qc.label_under_test: A second, mirrored labelling clause that casts the narrator: after one clause casts someone as something (sees him as a hero, calls her a liar), a following clause casts me or us (and she sees me as a nuisance, they treat us as outsiders); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after 'me'/'us', whoever does the labelling and whether or not the label is handed back. The same second clause aimed at him, her, you or them is weak, as is a one-way label of me with no earlier labelling clause, or me labelled in the first clause and answering back. Strongest when a sentence of setting comes first.

neighbours.label: A second, mirrored labelling clause that casts the speaker or the listener: after one clause casts someone as something (sees him as a hero, calls her a liar), a following clause casts me, us or you (and she sees me as a nuisance, they treat us as outsiders, and he calls you a snob); it fires on the 'as' or 'a' right after 'me'/'us'/'you'. 'You' fires when you did the first labelling (you treat them as family, and they treat you as staff); after 'I see him as...', a second clause casting you stays weak. The same second clause aimed at him, her or them is weak, as is a one-way label of me or you with no earlier labelling clause, or me labelled in the first clause and answering back. Strongest when a sentence of setting comes first.
fire: The office party was loud and crowded. My boss sees Daniel as a rising star, and she sees me as a nuisance.
We moved to the village last spring. The locals treat the old baker as one of their own, but they treat us as outsiders.
The meeting ran late again. You call him a genius, and he calls you a snob.
Rain fell all afternoon at the reunion. My aunt regards my cousin as the family success, while she regards me as a lost cause.
The tour bus pulled into the square. The guide treated the driver as an equal, yet he treated us as luggage.
It was the first week of term. The teachers saw Mia as a natural leader, and they saw me as a troublemaker.
The restaurant was packed that night. You treat the waiters as family, and they treat you as staff.
Snow had closed the roads for days. The neighbours called Tom a hero, but they called us a burden.
quiet: The office party was loud and crowded. My boss sees Daniel as a rising star, and she sees Paul as a nuisance.
We moved to the village last spring. The locals treat the old baker as one of their own, but they treat the newcomers as outsiders.
The meeting ran late again. You call him a genius, and he calls her a snob.
Rain fell all afternoon at the reunion. My aunt regards me as a lost cause.
The tour bus pulled into the square. The guide treated us as luggage the whole day.
It was the first week of term. The teachers saw me as a troublemaker, and I saw them as tyrants.
The restaurant was packed that night. I see the chef as a friend, and the waiters treat you as staff.
Snow had closed the roads for days. The neighbours called Tom a hero, but they called his sons a burden.

predictions: Blind test (label-only second author). Expect most fire items at 0.2-0.6; the riskiest are the non-reciprocal 'me' cases where a third party is labelled first (boss/Daniel, teachers/Mia), which probed 0.20-0.26 in exploration.
